title: The Bright and the Better: A Lecture on Novelty and Effectiveness
instructions: 阅读下面的文章，完成10道题目。题目类型包括单选、填空和判断正误/未提及。填空题答案必须来自原文，且不超过字数限制。所有题目和选项均为英文，解释为中文。本材料为模拟教学材料，不是官方雅思考试。
passage:
Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about a distinction that sounds simple but is surprisingly easy to miss: the difference between novelty and effectiveness. Novelty is about being new, different, or unusual. Effectiveness is about producing the result you actually want. A new idea can be exciting and still be ineffective. An old idea can be boring and still work very well. In this lecture, I will explain why we often confuse the two, and how to keep them separate when we make decisions.

Let me start with a story from a simulated school project. A group of teachers wanted to improve reading scores. One teacher suggested a brand-new app with games, badges, and daily challenges. The app was definitely novel. Students had never seen anything like it. Another teacher suggested something much less exciting: twenty minutes of silent reading every morning, with a simple log sheet. No games. No badges. Just reading. The team decided to try both for six weeks. At the end, the silent reading group showed a clear improvement in comprehension. The app group enjoyed the lessons more, but their scores did not improve much. The app was novel; the silent reading was effective. This does not mean apps are bad. It means novelty and effectiveness are different questions. A tool can be enjoyable and still fail to deliver the outcome you are measuring, and a plain routine can succeed precisely because it is focused on that outcome.

So why do we confuse them? There are three common reasons. First, novelty is easy to see. A new design, a new method, a new word—these stand out. Effectiveness is often invisible. You cannot see twenty minutes of quiet reading producing better comprehension until the test results arrive. Second, novelty gives us a social reward. When we introduce something new, people notice us. When we repeat something old, people may not. Third, we are often tired of routine. A new approach feels like a rest, even if it is not better. These three forces push us toward the exciting option, even when the quiet option is the one that works.

Now, I am not saying novelty is unimportant. Novelty can attract attention, and attention can be the first step toward change. However, novelty alone is not enough. We need to ask: Does this new thing actually help us reach our goal? If the answer is no, then the new thing is interesting but not effective. If the answer is yes, then we have something valuable, whether it is new or old. Attention may open the door, but evidence decides whether we should walk through it.

Let me give you a second example, this time from a simulated workplace. A company wanted to improve team communication. The manager introduced a new messaging platform with colorful channels and emojis. Everyone was excited for two weeks. Then people stopped using it. Why? Because the platform did not solve the real problem: team members did not know who was responsible for which task. A simpler solution—a shared task list with names and deadlines—was less exciting but far more effective. The manager learned an important lesson: a new tool cannot fix an unclear process. When the process itself is the problem, adding novelty only hides the confusion for a short time.

At this point, you might be thinking, “But sometimes we need novelty to stay motivated.” I agree. Motivation matters. Nevertheless, we should not let motivation replace measurement. If we only ask “Is it new?” we may miss the more important question: “Is it working?” A good decision-maker asks both questions, but in the right order. First, define the result you want. Second, consider whether a new approach is likely to produce that result. Third, if the new approach is not clearly better, choose the simpler or older approach that has evidence behind it. This order protects you from being led by excitement alone.

Some people argue that old methods are always safer. I disagree. Old methods can also be ineffective. The point is not old versus new. The point is evidence versus no evidence. A new method with strong evidence is better than an old method with none. An old method with strong evidence is better than a new method with none. So the real question is not “Is it new?” but “Do we have evidence that it works?” Evidence, not age, should guide the choice.

Let me summarize. Novelty is about being new. Effectiveness is about producing results. We often confuse them because novelty is visible, socially rewarding, and a relief from routine. However, novelty is not the same as effectiveness. To make better decisions, define your goal, ask whether the new approach will help, and look for evidence. If you do this, you will not be fooled by a bright new idea that does not actually work. Thank you. I am happy to take questions.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture, what is the main difference between novelty and effectiveness?
options: Novelty is about being new, while effectiveness is about producing the result you want.
Novelty is always better than effectiveness.
Effectiveness is only about being different.
Novelty and effectiveness mean the same thing.
answers: Novelty is about being new, while effectiveness is about producing the result you want.
questions.explanation: 原文明确指出：Novelty is about being new, different, or unusual. Effectiveness is about producing the result you actually want. 因此A正确。
questions.evidence: Novelty is about being new, different, or unusual. Effectiveness is about producing the result you actually want.

grammar.title: 转折、让步、同意与不同意；转述观点
grammar.explanation: 在英语中，表达转折常用 however, but, nevertheless；让步常用 although, even though, while；同意与不同意常用 I agree, I disagree, I'm not sure I agree；转述观点常用 The speaker argues that..., She believes that..., He disagrees with the idea that...。注意：转折词连接两个相反的意思；让步词表示“虽然……但是……”；转述时注意时态和人称的变化。
grammar.example: Some people argue that old methods are always safer. I disagree.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word: The app was new, ______ it did not improve scores.
questions.evidence: The app group enjoyed the lessons more, but their scores did not improve much.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word: ______ the method was old, it worked very well.
questions.evidence: An old idea can be boring and still work very well.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word: The new tool was exciting; ______, it did not solve the real problem.
questions.evidence: The manager learned an important lesson: a new tool cannot fix an unclear process.

questions.prompt: Choose the best phrase: ______ the speaker, novelty is not the same as effectiveness.
questions.evidence: Novelty is not the same as effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word: I ______ with the idea that old methods are always safer.
questions.evidence: Some people argue that old methods are always safer. I disagree.

questions.prompt: Choose the best word: She ______ that motivation matters.
questions.explanation: 转述第三人称单数观点，用believes。

questions.prompt: Choose the best word: ______ we have evidence, we should not choose the new method.
questions.evidence: If the new approach is not clearly better, choose the simpler or older approach that has evidence behind it.

questions.prompt: Choose the best phrase: The speaker ______ the view that novelty alone is enough.
questions.explanation: 表示不同意某观点用disagrees with。
questions.evidence: However, novelty alone is not enough.
